text: How are EU-funded projects turning the everyday car journeys that local residents already make into a bookable service for other travellers, so that thinly populated places with too few passengers to support frequent scheduled services still get a usable connection to the wider transport network?
reference_answer: Four projects treat the trips residents already drive as the missing service in places too thinly settled for frequent scheduled transport. LOCARP4EU assesses Ecov's roadside carpooling stations, in which street terminals, road signs and an IT system handling payment pair local drivers with waiting passengers without the driver having to register or commit to an itinerary or schedule, aimed at city outskirts and the remote fringes local authorities struggle to serve; it puts the locally carpoolable share at 5% of total passenger-kilometres. RIDE2RAIL makes shared rides a complementary mode that extends rail and public transport networks, harmonising real-time information on rail, public transport, ride-sharing and crowdsourcing behind Travel Companion features and a crowd-based Transport Service Provider, explicitly to reinforce offers in rural and low-demand areas and open access to high-capacity services, tested in Padua, Athens, Brno and Helsinki. Two successive projects of the same firm cover the two ends of that idea: the earlier KAROS feasibility project tuned carpooling to short-distance trips and mixed carpooling lines with mass transit lines into what it calls a new, efficient public transportation system, reporting more than 40.000 carpool trips and 244 low density towns reconnected to the mass transit system, while the later UNITE scales the platform, applying artificial intelligence to turn empty car seats into low-cost public-transport-like networks in low density areas, claiming a network extension and densification by a factor of 10 and a transport cost divided by 10, sold as Karos Territories to local transportation authorities and Karos Enterprise to companies.

text: What have EU-funded research projects learned about how the judges at the global courts that put individuals on trial for the gravest crimes of war and mass violence understand their own role in shaping the law through their rulings?
reference_answer: Two projects speak to this. INCRICO interviewed judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and found that they see their duties as going well beyond applying recognised rules of law: they also treat fact-finding, dispute settlement, law-making, case management and governance - and, to a lesser degree, protecting the interests and values of the international community - as part of their judicial function, and these self-understandings feed back into the Court's deliberations, the drafting of its judgments and its use of separate and dissenting opinions. EaRL asked the same question of the wider international criminal bench, combining a systematic reading of all 240 available judgements of international criminal and hybrid courts (the ICC, the ad hoc Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and Rwanda (ICTR), and the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL)) with over 40 in-depth interviews with judges, civil-society staff and government representatives, and traced empirically how routine practices of legal interpretation come to produce new legal meaning. Taken together, the two projects describe a bench that regards developing the law as one of its own achievements, and both look outward as well - INCRICO at how the Court's judgments are received as authoritative, EaRL at how a wider interpretive community of government officials, NGOs and other international courts takes up those decisions.

text: How do the aims differ between projects that study the woodwork of ships that sank centuries ago - what does each team hope those old ship timbers can tell them?
reference_answer: Both projects read the wood of ships that went down centuries ago, but they ask opposite kinds of question of it. ModernShip Project works on the structural remains of 16th-century wrecks of Mediterranean build - Mortella (1527, France) and Santiago de Galicia (1597, Spain), alongside the already documented Lomellina and Calvi I - in order to draft, for the first time, a Mediterranean technical model of how such ships were put together and to set it against the better-known Atlantic one, so that the continuous exchanges and technological transfers between the two nautical spaces can be described. TIMBER treats ship timber instead as precisely dated evidence about a resource: tree-ring work on the Swedish warship Vasa, built in Stockholm in 1628 and sunk on her first voyage in Stockholm Harbour, confirmed timbers from at least four distinct sources, including a Baltic and a west Swedish source, alongside purchase records naming eastern Sweden, Riga, Koenigsberg and Amsterdam, showing that even in heavily forested Sweden timber was imported from abroad. On the Boele Ship, a wreck dated to the 1380s found in the river Skienselva in southern Norway that sank with a cargo of whetstones from Eidsborg, every timber analysed - the keel included - came from the southern Baltic around the mouth of the Vistula River, which TIMBER reads not as evidence for the transport of timber but as a ship built at the Vistula mouth; both cases feed its account of the maritime timber trade from c. AD 1100 to 1700, with felling dates and regions of origin. The difference is what the wood is evidence for: for ModernShip it is evidence of design and construction practice in two coexisting technical cultures, for TIMBER it is evidence of where trees were felled, who traded them and how timber moved.

text: Some EU projects build solar-fuel photoelectrodes out of carbon nitride rather than a metal-based semiconductor, so they have to work out how to make the material themselves. How do those projects differ in the routes they use to produce and deposit the carbon nitride layer?
reference_answer: MFreePEC works bottom-up from the molecule: it encodes the composition of a family of metal-free CNX materials (X = P, B or S) into supramolecular precursors, uses the stable intermediate melem to synthesise CN photoanodes in the 5-20 min range at higher temperatures, and gets the layer onto transparent conductive electrodes by electrophoretic deposition, ultrasonic spray of precursors, doctor-blading, dip-coating and added precursor vapour pressure during calcination - a porous carbon-nitride photoanode containing reduced graphene oxide and a nickel-iron oxyhydroxide oxidation co-catalyst held photocurrents exceeding 0.45 mA/cm2 at 1.23 V vs. NHE for more than 35 h. CALSOL instead pits two whole synthesis routes against each other for its carbon-based artificial leaf - the traditional thermal polycondensation route and a plasma polymerization route - and its headline result is negative about the traditional one: the product of thermal polycondensation of melamine is not graphitic carbon nitride but a defective melon structure that degraded considerably during photoelectrochemical experiments, with a flatband potential drifting from approx. -1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl to -1.8 vs. Ag/AgCl across pH. The contrast is therefore between engineering precursor chemistry and deposition method to build a durable working photoanode (MFreePEC) and testing whether an established preparation route yields a usable carbon nitride photoelectrode material at all (CALSOL).

text: Several EU projects set out to turn software that writes music by itself into something they could sell. How did they differ in what that software was meant to do for its intended users?
reference_answer: I2C8 turned the Lrn2Cre8 FET project's machine-learning work into a digital audio workstation plug-in for chord sequence generation, pitched to electronic musicians, producers and DJs as a 'musical sketchpad'; it deliberately stays small - predominantly sequences of up to eight chords - because its stated aim is to 'inspire' for composing, not to deliver complete compositions. AIVA, an AI that trained itself on 30,000+ classical music pieces, went the other way and offered content creators finished royalty-free soundtracks 'in the matter of seconds, and at the touch of a button', transitioning from a service to an embeddable Music Engine plus an API that lets third-party developers create hundreds of hours of soundtrack music, and it validated commercial feasibility by testing users' response and willingness to pay for the Music Engine public beta released in the second half of 2019. CALMUSgaming, from the Icelandic SME ErkiTónlist and built on its CALMUS technology, targeted computer games instead: its report says the software generates new background music as the game evolves, with minimal contribution from the composer, saving up to 90% of the time devoted to music composition, and the funded work was a feasibility study covering technical scope, markets and competition, a patent search and a 5-year financial forecast. FlowMachines, a PoC of the ERC Flow-Machines project, treated musical style itself as the asset to sell and set out to build a style manipulation prototype for the music synchronization business - music composed to be synchronized to existing media such as advertisements, movie music or video games - but its report concludes that 'Direct commercial exploitation of AI technologies per se is no longer a profitable route', that the team shifted to producing, distributing and monetizing content by the music industry's 'traditional means', and that they convinced top executives of a major music label to create a dedicated label specialized in the production and dissemination of music composed with AI technologies; on the legal side it catalogued the copyright issues in a report but 'considered that it was not worth addressing the issues raised by each copyright type'.

text: Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?
reference_answer: EU-funded research on this question sits mostly in political economy, and it covers both who does the influencing and what it achieves. Several projects put firms at the centre of trade rule-making: PROSPER studies firms that 'mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union' and reports that because 'particularly resourceful firms are able to carry their political demands to policymakers, interest representation might be skewed in their favor'; TRASC builds a firm-level dataset of lobbying on the ratification and content of free trade agreements and on antidumping measures; DIA reports that the effect of industry lobbying on international rule-making depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests. Other projects work on domestic policy: BUSWEL compares the policy positions and strategies of business interest groups in Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria and the United States and, as delivered, focused on three policy fields - corporate taxation, inheritance taxation and wage bargaining - finding that the responsiveness of governments to business demands depends on the policy at hand and on the types of firms represented; MILO models how polluting firms' incentives to join a lobby group shape a policy maker's choice of environmental policy instrument; BIZPOL maps corporate political activity, 'all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests'. The set reaches further sectors and periods: POWERSHIFTS finds that 'firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation' and that 'incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes'; MIGPSC asks how private security actors and the defence industry shape European migration management policy; GRIP-ARM asks how business power shapes the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries; EFTA DEVELOPMENT traces how non-state actors including business lobby groups shaped EFTA's policies and priorities between 1958 and 1992; EURECON studies the influence of non-state actors including commercial banks and big business on European economic decision-making; and ClimActiv and CORPORATOCRACY treat corporate lobbying and corporate political power as questions of democratic legitimacy rather than of measurement.
notes: Seeds: PROSPER 842868 and LOBFRAM 657949 from the corpus-profile candidate (social sciences/political sciences bucket), read before the question existed; the question was composed from PROSPER's 'firms ... influence trade policymaking' and LOBFRAM's 'non-state actors (NSAs), such as business groups'. Candidate drift check (first pass): the candidate's in-bucket lobbying cluster re-executes to 9 members, not 5; corpus-wide there are 17 projects with 'lobb' in project.objective and 84 with 'lobb' in objective or any report_text section, so the euroSciVoc fence was dropped and gold was built corpus-wide. GOLD RULE (tightened this pass): IN iff the project's own research, as stated in its objective or its published report sections, examines efforts to influence public policy, regulation or rule-making AND the influencing actor is identified in the project's own text as business, firms, corporate or industry. OUT: the project's own advocacy or dissemination; passing background mentions; an influence claim attributed only to a cited literature rather than to the project's own findings; influencers named only as lobbies, special interests, interest groups or lobbyists with no business identification; and the reverse direction (regulation acting on an industry). The tightened rule changed three cases this pass: CITIZINGLOBAL 714905 dropped from gold (its texts say 'lobbies' and 'powerful special interests', never business/firms/corporate/industry - the same ground on which CONSERVATION 683031 was already out); PARTICIPATE 948516 dropped from gold (its own delivered finding is the tax-price elasticity of corporate giving, and the influence claim 'corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics' is explicitly attributed to 'the recent literature on tax-exempt lobbying'); SPIKE 797989 adjudicated and named OUT (it studies the US lobbying industry itself - 'quantify the importance of lobbyist-client relationships' - and aims to inform 'the regulation of advocacy services', not business influence on policy). The four other previously disclosed weak members were re-run under the same rule and stay IN because each names a business actor in its own text: UneqDems 741538 ('the exercise of business power in switzerland'), IFDG 786587 ('us firms react more to increased competition from china by lobbying more'), GRIP-ARM 950056 ('how do state capacity, business power and organizational structure of domestic markets shape the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries?'), CORPORATOCRACY 865165 ('Business corporations exercise political power, both internally ... and externally (towards states, consumers and others)'). POWERSHIFTS 751843 added to gold: its own report finds 'Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits' and 'Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes', and its workPerformed reports that renewable energy communities build political coalitions 'most often with renewables companies and industry groups'. Pooling arithmetic: 43 candidates were pooled across the four conditions at k=20; 5 of them are gold (BUSWEL 705677, PROSPER 842868, TRASC 834253, BIZPOL 840978, LOBFRAM 657949) and the other 38 were rejected, so pooled_candidate_count 43 = 5 pooled-and-accepted + rejected_count 38. The `accepted` field carries all 16 gold ids because the brief requires accepted == gold_project_ids; the 11 gold that are not in that 5 were never in the pool at all - they were found by the SQL completeness sweeps below. Completeness sweeps, all executed and all fully enumerated: (S1) '\blobb' over project.objective - 17 rows, all adjudicated; (S2) '\blobb' over report_text teaser/summary/workPerformed/finalResults for projects S1 missed - 67 rows, all triaged from a 140-char context window; (S3) actor-first proximity (business|corporate|corporation|industry|industries|firm|company) NEAR (lobb|influenc|captur|shap|press) NEAR (polic|regulat|legislat|rule-making|government) over objective+report - 29 rows, all read; (S4) '(regulatory capture|corporate political|business interest group|business power|producer group|interest group NEAR influenc/lobb/polic/legislat)' - 7 rows, all read; (S5, this pass, closing the directional blind spot S3 left) the same actor/verb/policy proximity in BOTH word orders - actor-first and policy-first - with the verb set widened to (lobb|influenc|captur|shap|press|oppos|resist|block|push|campaign|advocat|sway|persuad), gaps of up to 70 non-sentence-ending characters, over objective plus all four report sections, excluding the 73 projects already adjudicated: 58 rows, every one returned and read. All 58 are OUT. The recurring patterns are the reverse direction, regulation pressuring an industry (GRAIL 638719, iLABOUR 639652, TyRec 672558, HEAT-R 697982, Auxilia 775737, Triboconditioning 823307, CLIMEX 851876, FinanceCC 885552, LAND GRIFFON 101004174); the project's own dissemination or advocacy (PV FINANCING 646554, progRESsHEAT 646573, SmartAct-2-3 650702, FloTEC 691916, InnoRenew CoE 739574, IFASA 744848, AQUA-FAANG 817923, RESTORE 820292, CASCADES 821010, SENSEI 847066, 5GMED 951947, EU-PolarNet 2 101003766); stakeholder or audience lists (SLALOM 644270, BeLEADFREE 691503, CineAF 891966); and false positives on device or process vocabulary ('pressure regulator': M-H70 826062, P200 876347; CO2 'capture': ACCSESS 101022487). Three S5 rows were read in full before rejection: MANAGLOBAL 823744 (local management practice and 'private companies' government' in African and Arab countries - corporate governance, not public policy), FASHION IN IR 886026 (the influence of French women's fashion on the American mass market and within the common market, not business influence on government policy), RECENT 823903 (beyond-5G wireless networks; the hit is an impact sentence about consortium companies and technical standards). S5 produced no new gold beyond POWERSHIFTS 751843, which the judge supplied. term_style paraphrase, recounted this pass by SQL over objective plus all report sections: 10 of the 16 gold texts carry a 'lobb' token as their key term (LOBFRAM, EFTA DEVELOPMENT, MILO, IFDG, MIGPSC, DIA, TRASC, BIZPOL, PROSPER, ClimActiv) and 6 do not (BUSWEL, EURECON, UneqDems, POWERSHIFTS, CORPORATOCRACY, GRIP-ARM), while the question uses none of that vocabulary, saying 'try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt'; consistent with the rank matrix, where only BUSWEL (lexical 8), PROSPER (lexical 13) and LOBFRAM (lexical 17) reach the lexical top-20 and the rest of the pooled gold arrives via dense/hybrid/rerank. Named near-misses left OUT: CITIZINGLOBAL 714905, PARTICIPATE 948516 and SPIKE 797989 (reasons above), REVEAL 725798 (resilience of private rule-making bodies, not efforts to shape government policy), TRADEPOWER 724107 (bargaining power of countries in trade negotiations), POLBUSNETWORKS 724501 (firm-politician favour networks and misallocation), CLIFF 101020082 ('fossil fuel vested interests are lobbying heavily' is scene-setting), Digital Good 804985 (one workPerformed bullet), IMPACT HAU 772544 (lobbyists named among ethnographic case sites), CONSERVATION 683031 (lobbyists unspecified, in a resource-conservation game-theory paper), ENERGY ETHICS 715146 ('the strong industry lobbies' as context), PmNC 832350 and DemocInChange 702134 and DEMSEC 639021 and CONSULTATIONEFFECTS 804288 (civil society or interest groups not identified as business), Dia-Pol 101028566 (activists), CitIndus 890615 and WELTECH 101033625 (background phrases), FEDCIT 740447 (lobbying by municipalities), PEMP 637662 (lobbying listed as a future application). Remaining doubt: GRIP-ARM 950056 and CORPORATOCRACY 865165 still rest mainly on their objectives - both are ongoing and their interim reports do not repeat the phrase - so they are the two members most exposed to a stricter report-only reading.

text: What separation-management approaches for drone traffic have European U-space projects developed themselves - their own methods for keeping drones apart and resolving conflicts - as opposed to demonstrating separation services supplied by others?

pooling_evidence.note: single pooled run at k=40 over the final wording; 57 distinct pooled projects = 9 accepted-from-pool + 48 rejected. 776293 GAUSS is gold but retrieved by no condition at k=40; its provenance is the completeness sweep, recorded here rather than folded into the pooled arithmetic. hybrid_rerank returns 20 projects (reranker stage cap), the other three conditions 40.

reference_answer: European work on U-space separation splits between designing the separation service itself and validating deconfliction technology in flight. BUBBLES formulates a U-Space advanced (U3) separation management service at TRL3, computing UAS collision risk so that separation minima and methods - procedural, tactical self-separated or tactical ground-based - can be derived from a stated probability of collision. USEPE studies separation methods for demanding environments such as cities and applies machine learning to automate safe separation and deconfliction while holding airspace capacity. Metropolis 2 treats airspace design, flight planning and separation management as interdependent at high traffic density, comparing concepts that differ in how separation is performed (strategic/tactical, ground/air) by simulation before a real-world demonstration, while DACUS embeds separation management in a Demand and Capacity Balancing process and searches for the optimal balance between on-board separation intelligence and U-space separation service intelligence. LABYRINTH takes the centralised route, computing 4D paths for drone swarms so trajectories do not collide. On the technology and demonstration side, CLASS matured ground-based tracking with tactical deconfliction tools that suggest new conflict-free trajectories; IMPETUS tested tactical de-confliction in which virtual weights attached to each drone define the separation criteria, giving dynamic separation; TINDAiR demonstrated AI-based tactical deconfliction with a detect-and-avoid service over VTOL flights; GOF2.0 validated an architecture for highly automated real-time separation assurance in dense urban airspace; and GAUSS approaches coordination among UAS through Galileo-EGNOS precise positioning plus tactical deconfliction services in its UTM system.
notes: Membership criterion is now STATED IN THE QUESTION: a project is gold iff its own stored text shows it developed or validated its own method for keeping drones apart or resolving conflicts between them (separation minima, strategic or tactical deconfliction, conflict detection and resolution) within U-space/UTM; a project that only demonstrates or consumes a separation-type service supplied by partners is excluded by the question's own words ('as opposed to demonstrating separation services supplied by others'), as is on-board sensing hardware and manned-aviation separation work. The earlier 'large numbers of drones' qualifier was dropped because gold members TINDAiR (largest exercise: 'Deconfliction between an autonomous drone, an eVTOL carrying a passenger and a manned helicopter') and GAUSS ('4 UTM coordinated RPAS') do not satisfy it. IN (10): 890378 USEPE ('research on drones' separation methods in high demanding environments such as cities', ML for separation and deconfliction); 892928 Metropolis 2 (unified approach to airspace design and separation management; strategic/tactical deconfliction, dynamic capacity management; compares its own separation concepts by simulation); 893206 BUBBLES (formulation and validation of a U3 separation management service, own collision-risk algorithms, separation minima and methods); 893864 DACUS (own DCB process integrating separation management, on-board vs U-space separation intelligence); 861696 LABYRINTH (own centralized 4D path-planning system computing paths to avoid collisions for drone swarms under U-SPACE); 101017677 TINDAiR (own AI-based tactical deconfliction demonstrated in flight, Tactical Conflict Resolution and DAA); 101017689 GOF2.0 (own GOF 2.0 architecture for highly automated real-time separation assurance; trials driven by strategic deconfliction); 763719 CLASS (own ground-based UTMS with tactical deconfliction - 'Airbus teams investigated deconfliction by adapting available algorithms from manned aviation. The traffic simulator and the conflict detection have been tuned to drone characteristics'); 763807 IMPETUS (own tactical de-confliction concept tested, virtual weights defining separation criteria for dynamic separation); 776293 GAUSS (objective: 'coordination among a higher number of RPAS' and 'the definition, negotiation and execution of safe trajectories'; finalResults: 'Development of algorithms and functionalities for U-space in-flight services ... such as UTM simulators and tactical deconfliction services' - mechanism is Galileo/EGNOS positioning rather than a separation algorithm, which the reference states). Demonstrator cases resolved explicitly under the stated criterion, all OUT: 783230 PODIUM (self-described 'U-Space compliant demonstration'; its finalResults report evidence on partners' services 'including drone registration and identification, automatic flight plan validation ... and conflict detection and alerting' - it evaluates services it did not develop); 101017701 SAFIR-Med ('leveraged to make use of the maximum number of U-Space services ..., including advanced Detect And Avoid U-space service'); 101017682 CORUS-XUAM (VLD campaigns in which 'Vertiport procedures, separation, and data services will be also demonstrated' using partners' U-space deployments); 101017643 Uspace4UAM (VLD demonstrations with 'a well experienced UTM provider'); 783261 USIS (demonstrates a list of initial U-space services - e-identification, tracking, flight planning, monitoring). Other OUT: 783211 SAFEDRONE and 763702 PercEvite (on-board sense/detect-and-avoid technology, not a traffic-separation method); 861211 RAPID (on-board sense-and-detect for inspection drones); 894593 ICARUS (common altitude reference; its separation is drone-to-ground-obstacle and drone-to-manned vertical); 734143 PJ10 PROSA, 874464 PJ10-W2 PROSA, 699247 R-WAKE, 101017688 VLD2-VOICE, 699337 SALSA, 892919 SafeOPS, 699299 DART, 699249 COMPAIR, 890417 ECHO, 699313 AGENT (manned-aviation separation/collision avoidance: AGENT extends TCAS for aircraft and ATC, no drones, no U-space); 870251 DELOREAN, 783228 GAINS, 791438 Aerobits, 763601 DroC2om, 763658 AIRPASS, 857031 5G!Drones, 826610 COMP4DRONES, 827563 TRANSDAT (navigation, communication, avionics or visibility enablers, no separation method); 763551 CORUS, 763671 DREAMS, 763831 TERRA, 101017521 PJ34-W3 AURA, 763599 SECOPS, 101017702 AMU-LED, 101007134 AURORA, 892440 URClearED, 867479 AIRCARRUS, 861635 5D-AeroSafe, 663483 ADS Project, 870236 HUUVER, 955317 FRONTIER, 777465 X2RAIL-2, 887092 WINGPULSE, 832537 GASTEJO, 753561 GINGER, 892054 ComAct, 690959 Errspitals, 847118 FEASIBLE, 747947 EU-Drones (concept/information/policy work, non-aviation, or lexical noise). Sweeps (unchanged, first round): objective LIKE '%u-space%' -> 19 projects; chunk text LIKE '%u-space%' OR '%uspace%' -> 43 projects with per-project counts of chunks containing separat/deconflict/conflict resolution/detect and avoid, every non-zero one read; non-U-space net (drone|uas|unmanned a|utm|urban air mobility) x (separation|deconflict|conflict resolution|detect and avoid|traffic management) -> 14 projects, all OUT except CLASS and IMPETUS. term_style re-derived from the new wording: exact-term - the question reuses 'separation management', 'U-space', 'drone traffic' and 'conflicts' verbatim from the gold titles and objectives, and lexical ranks 8 of the 10 gold in its top-40 (DACUS 1, USEPE 2, CLASS 3, Metropolis 2 4, TINDAiR 5, IMPETUS 7, BUBBLES 10, LABYRINTH 26), with GOF2.0 dense-only (22) and GAUSS unretrieved.
